lyrics:
[Intro: lone lead guitar arpeggio riff, band enters one by one]

[Verse 1: soft, sweet, raspy]
Her laugh is a screen door slamming
On the first warm night of the year
And every time I hear it coming
All my winters disappear

[Chorus: wide wailing vocal]
Oh, oh, Little Thunder
Don't you ever quiet down
Oh, oh, Little Thunder
Shake the windows of this town

[Verse 2: soft, sweet, raspy]
Her look is a storm deciding
If it's gonna break or pass
I'd stand out in a field forever
Just to watch it cross the grass

[Chorus: wide wailing vocal]
Oh, oh, Little Thunder
Don't you ever quiet down
Oh, oh, Little Thunder
Shake the windows of this town

[Guitar Solo: short, melodic, sings the vocal line]

[Verse 3: soft, sweet]
Her hands are small but they move the weather
Her heart's a drum the sky can't hold
And if the world should try to hush her
I'll be her echo when I'm old

[Chorus: wide wailing vocal]
Oh, oh, Little Thunder
Don't you ever quiet down
Oh, oh, Little Thunder
Shake the windows of this town

[Guitar Solo: long, lyrical, then wah pedal, screaming bend]

[Breakdown: turns minor, half-time, palm mutes, builds to screams]
What do we do with all this time?
What do we do with it now?
What do we do (what do we do)
What do we do with all this sky?
What do we do with all this time?
(Little Thunder, Little Thunder)
What do we do with it now?

[Outro: full band crescendo, final chord rings out]
Roll on, roll on
Roll on, Little Thunder
Roll on
producerBrief:
TEMPO / KEY / FEEL: 122 BPM, 4/4, E major for the body of the song, shifting to E minor for the final breakdown. Bright and affectionate for three minutes, then dark and searching.

VOICE: Male high tenor with a serrated rasp, sweet and almost lullaby-soft in the verses, opening into a wide, wailing upper register on the chorus 'oh, oh'. Low octave double on the breakdown questions, building to full-throated screams at the end.

INSTRUMENTS: Lead electric guitar on the neck pickup through a cranked British tube amp, playing a circular, string-skipping arpeggio riff that sounds like a music box played by a rock band (the earworm). A second rhythm guitar with crunchy open chords. Melodic bass that answers the riff in the intro. Big live drums with a cracking snare and wide tom fills. No keyboards.

ARRANGEMENT MAP: 0:00 Intro, the arpeggio riff alone, then bass melody, then rhythm guitar and drums entering one at a time over 30 seconds. 0:31 Verse 1. 0:47 Chorus 1. 1:03 Verse 2. 1:19 Chorus 2. 1:35 Guitar solo 1, short and melodic, singing the vocal line. 1:51 Verse 3. 2:07 Chorus 3. 2:23 Guitar solo 2, the big one: starts lyrical, kicks on a wah pedal, climbs the neck, ends on a screaming sustained bend. 2:55 Breakdown, the key turns minor, half-time feel, chugging palm mutes, the question repeated and intensifying. 3:40 Outro, full-band crescendo on 'roll on', final crashing chord rings out to 4:05.

PRODUCTION & MIX: Live-in-a-room energy. Guitars panned left and right, natural room reverb on the drums, vocal upfront with a short slap delay, minimal polish.

SIGNATURE MOMENT: The intro riff. Two notes in, the whole room knows the song. Second place goes to the instant the key turns minor.

MODERN POINT OF VIEW: Tighter, deeper low end than a 1987 master, and parallel-compressed drums for punch on small speakers. The breakdown's low vocal double is close and dry, like a private thought.

EMOTIONAL ARC: Adoration, celebration, then the ache of time passing.

WHAT IT IS ABOUT

A love song to someone small, loud and unstoppable, whose laugh ends winters. The singer promises to be her echo, then is left asking what to do with all the time that is passing.

THE OTHER WAYS TO HEAR IT

Hear it as: a father to a daughter; a lover to a firecracker partner; an adult talking to the fearless kid they used to be; or a tribute to anyone the world tried to quieten. The breakdown ('what do we do with all this time?') is a parent watching a child grow, or anyone facing the second half of life.

ENGINEERED HOOKS AND THE DESIGNED MISHEARING

Borrowed mechanics: nature similes that anchor love in memory, a rough voice singing soft words, and a late turn from major-key comfort to a minor-key unanswered question. Designed mishearing: 'Little Thunder' is heard as 'Little Wonder', and both fit. The nickname is built to be given to real children, pets and guitars.
